# From transcript to protein

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/11-transcript-to-protein.yml` and not yet reviewed by a
second reader.
:::

@sec-ends established where isoform differences sit in a transcript. Most sit at
the start of
the coding sequence, at the end, or outside the reading frame, rather than in
the middle.

The next question is what such a difference does to the protein.
Three answers all turn up often: the protein changes at one end, its sequence
stays the same while the amount made changes, or the transcript yields no
protein at all.

## The mechanism predicts which part of the protein changes {#sec-what-changes}

The mechanism is largely predictable from the region of the protein affected,
and establishing that took a systematic comparison. Across
35,082 pairs of annotated human protein isoforms, differences at the beginning
of the protein came overwhelmingly from the gene starting transcription
somewhere else. That accounted for 70 per cent of them. Splicing inside the 5'
UTR accounted for 9 per cent [@murali2025biosurfer].

Differences at the other end of the protein had a different cause. There, 72 per
cent involved a shift in reading frame, introduced either by a splice or by a
retained intron [@murali2025biosurfer]. The two ends of a protein are reached by
different routes.

![What produces a difference depends on where in the protein the difference
sits. Proportions are of annotated isoform pairs, so they describe the
annotation as much as the
biology.](../figures/mechanism-by-region.svg){#fig-mechanism-region width=100%}

A third mechanism operates between the two ends. A codon can straddle a splice
junction, with one or two of its bases in the upstream exon and the rest in the
downstream one. Splicing to a different partner then rebuilds
that codon from different pieces and changes a single amino acid, without
inserting or deleting anything. Those authors found this behind 17 per cent of
internal sequence changes and called the pattern ragged codons
[@murali2025biosurfer]. A one-residue difference is not the kind of change an
event-level metric is built to report; @sec-psi gives what that metric does
measure.

Running the same comparison on a proteome predicted from long reads of a human
cell line showed similar trends, with one difference: more of the transcripts
were predicted to be destroyed rather than translated [@murali2025biosurfer].
That is a hint about what long reads add to this question, and
@sec-is-it-translated takes it up.

## Differences that touch no amino acid {#sec-utr-only}

An isoform pair can differ in no amino acid whatsoever. This is the common case,
and the regulatory consequences are real but smaller and less consistent than
the literature's enthusiasm suggests.

### The five-prime leader

Start-site choice changes the length of the untranslated leader, and the leader
affects how efficiently a ribosome gets going. Measured directly in mouse
fibroblasts by separating isoforms with different start sites and asking how
many ribosomes each carried, 4,153 of 9,951 expressed genes initiated at more
than one site. Of those, 745 translated their isoforms at detectably different
rates [@wang2016alttss]. The direction was consistent: the isoform with the
longer leader was generally translated less well. Sequence features inside the
leaders explained over half the variance in that difference, which leaves a
substantial remainder unexplained [@wang2016alttss].

One result undercuts the premise of this section. The length of the leader can
set which protein is made as well as how much, by controlling which start codon
the ribosome uses. A very short
leader lets the ribosome slide past the first available start codon, so the
shorter protein form is the one produced [@ly2026utrlength]. Because start-site
choice sets leader length, moving the start site shifts the ratio between two
protein forms without altering a single base of coding sequence
[@ly2026utrlength].

That mechanism reaches inherited disease, and a deletion inside the VHL leader
was found to push translation toward the shorter of that gene's two protein
forms [@ly2026utrlength]. A variant in an untranslated region changed a protein,
and any pipeline that filters variants to the coding sequence would discard it.
@sec-vus covers how clinical interpretation handles variants that act through
splicing.

### The three-prime tail

The three-prime untranslated region is where the field most often asserts
consequence and most often disagrees about it.

Measured genome-wide in one mouse cell line, the choice between a near and a far
polyadenylation site did very little. Isoforms using the far site were slightly
less stable and slightly better translated, the effects ran in opposite
directions, and the strongest element found was the microRNA site, associated
with 32 per cent repression of stability against only 4 per cent of translation
[@spies2013utrisoform]. The authors' own summary was that in those cells
alternative tails mattered less than other parts of the transcript, because the
two isoforms of a gene behaved alike [@spies2013utrisoform].

One gene studied closely gave the opposite answer, and in the opposite direction
from the obvious prediction. PTEN transcripts carrying the longest tails, and
therefore the most microRNA sites, were the stable ones, resisted silencing, and
supplied most of the protein [@thivierge2018ptenapa]. Those authors drew a
methodological conclusion from it. A microRNA site validated in a gene's
untranslated region may not act on the isoforms that actually carry that gene's
output [@thivierge2018ptenapa].

A third result suggests when the choice matters, though it does not settle the
disagreement. Arsenic exposure shortened tails across the transcriptome by two
separate routes, a shift toward the near site during the stress and selective
destruction of the long forms during recovery [@zheng2018stressapa]. TIA1 binds
uracil-rich stretches that exist only in the extended part of the tail, and that
binding correlates with stress granule association and with decay of the long
forms [@zheng2018stressapa]. The consequence inverts the usual intuition about
regulatory elements. Carrying fewer of them is protective, because a transcript
that had already switched to the near site survived the clean-up
[@zheng2018stressapa].

The summary is therefore conditional, and rests on few systems. In unstressed
mouse fibroblasts, which tail a gene uses was mostly inconsequential. Under
stress, and at one gene whose dosage is tightly held, it mattered a great
deal. @sec-sc-apa gives the cell-type
dimension of the same choice.

## Evidence that an annotated isoform reaches protein {#sec-is-it-translated}

@sec-how-functional sets out the three-way disagreement about how much
alternative splicing matters. Protein-level evidence bears on it directly, and
it has arrived from two independent directions.

Ribosome footprints assigned to individual isoforms rather than pooled per gene
found evidence of translation for 40 to 50 per cent of expressed isoforms. More
than one isoform was translated at 53 per cent of expressed human genes and 33
per cent of mouse genes [@reixachs2020orqas]. Agreement between the two levels
was partial: about 40 per cent of the splicing changes visible in RNA were
matched by a change in translation [@reixachs2020orqas]. The changes that did
carry through were disproportionately microexons, and for exons that correspond
between human and mouse the direction of change was preserved
[@reixachs2020orqas]. That microexon result matters later, because @sec-rps24 is
a microexon case.

Mass spectrometry reached the question by a different route, and had to be
pushed unusually hard to do it. A routine proteomics run reads only a fraction
of each protein, which is why it cannot tell two isoforms apart
[@sinitcyn2023deepproteome]. The depth required came from splitting six cell
lines with six different enzymes and reading the fragments three ways, which
yielded a million peptides from 17,717 protein groups and covered a median of
about 80 per cent of each protein's length [@sinitcyn2023deepproteome].

![The same measurement supports two different headlines depending on which genes
are counted. Detection of alternative junctions in protein rises with how well
the gene is covered.](../figures/translated-denominator.svg){#fig-translated width=100%}

The result is usually quoted as settling whether splicing diversity reaches the
proteome, and that quotation needs its denominator. Across everything
compared against RNA, about 80 per cent of single-residue variants were seen in
protein but only about 20 per cent of the junctions expected from splicing
[@sinitcyn2023deepproteome]. Restricted to genes expressed highly enough to be
read end to end, detection of frame-preserving splicing events rose to about 64
per cent [@sinitcyn2023deepproteome].

The load-bearing comparison is a different one. In those well-covered genes,
alternative junctions were detected about as often as constitutive ones
[@sinitcyn2023deepproteome]. An alternative isoform is harder to find only
because it is scarcer. On that reading the low overall rate measures the assay,
and the conclusion that most frame-preserving alternative isoforms are
translated follows [@sinitcyn2023deepproteome].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why some variants never appear in protein

For the single-residue variants that were expected from RNA and never seen in
protein, those authors offered a mechanism rather than filing them as a
measurement failure. Those variants were predicted more often to destabilise the
protein [@sinitcyn2023deepproteome]. If that is right, absence from the proteome
is a biological result about protein stability and not a gap in coverage. It also
means the proteome is not a straightforward readout of the transcriptome even
when both are measured well.
:::

## RPS24: one codon at the end of a ribosomal protein {#sec-rps24}

Most of this chapter is about proportions across thousands of genes. One small
gene shows the whole argument at once.

The RPS24 gene contributes a protein to the small ribosomal subunit. Between two
exons that are always present, it carries three very short exons of 3, 18 and 22
base pairs [@park2024rps24]. They sit at the end of the coding sequence, so
including or excluding them changes the last few amino acids rather than an
internal domain [@park2024rps24]. The three-base-pair exon is one codon, so a
gene can add or remove a single residue by a splicing decision.

![The RPS24 locus and the protein ends its documented isoforms produce. The
three-base-pair exon is drawn to scale against its neighbours.](../figures/rps24-microexons.svg){#fig-rps24 width=100%}

The difference falls on the protein's last few residues. The exon of 22 base
pairs carries a stop codon, so a transcript including it ends the protein
three residues early. The form that excludes it keeps a proline, a lysine and a
glutamate that the other lacks [@kerry2024rps24hypoxia]. The published naming
scheme labels the protein forms by what they end in, which is two lysines, three
lysines, or proline-lysine-glutamate [@magadi2025rps24].

Lysine is a plausible place for this to matter, because lysines are where cells
attach the tags that control a protein's fate. Those authors raise
ubiquitination and acetylation as possibilities and do not demonstrate either
[@kerry2024rps24hypoxia]. Where the protein sits gives a second reason for
interest. It lies beside the channel through which messenger RNA enters the
ribosome [@magadi2025rps24].

### Five incompatible naming schemes for one gene {#sec-rps24-naming}

Reading these papers together runs into a wall. The groups do not label the gene
the same way. Junction names
and transcript names and protein names were each introduced by different authors
for the same molecules, and a scheme published specifically to reconcile them
reports that no previous system distinguished the proteins at all
[@magadi2025rps24].

Part of the problem is not editorial, since the reference databases number this
gene's exons differently from one transcript to the next [@magadi2025rps24].
Transcript length and protein length also run in opposite directions here, and
the shortest transcript encodes the longest protein [@magadi2025rps24].

This book does not assert a single table mapping each exon combination to each
protein end. Reconciling the schemes means tracking the exon numbering each
paper used, and the published reconciliation cannot be followed unambiguously
from its own text. Settling it would take the annotated transcript and protein
sequences rather than the papers. Each result below is therefore reported in its
own paper's labels.

### Tissue proportions that are conserved between species {#sec-rps24-regulation}

The proportions differ by tissue, and by tumour type within a tissue
[@park2024rps24]. One combination behaves like a tissue marker that disease
removes: abundant in muscle, present in normal brain, absent from glioma
[@park2024rps24]. Across the three forms, one predominates in heart, another in
brain, and the third across blood and the solid organs [@magadi2025rps24].

Two independent lines of evidence say this is held in place. The
proportions in brain are nearly identical in mouse and human
[@magadi2025rps24]. In a survey of splicing across twelve human tissues, RPS24
was one of a small minority of genes whose splicing tracked tissue
compartment consistently, with one of the largest such effects measured
[@olivieri2021splicing].

The same survey produced a sharper result. The splicing of RPS24 and one other
gene was enough on its own, with no use of
expression level, to sort individual human cells into the right tissue
compartment [@olivieri2021splicing]. @sec-sc-structure gives the accuracies, the
two genes behind that result are RPS24 and ATP5F1C, and the same compartment
pattern was found again in mouse and in mouse lemur [@olivieri2021splicing].

### Consequences under hypoxia and in the brain {#sec-rps24-consequence}

The two protein forms are not equally durable, and the difference appears only
under stress. They lasted equally long in normal oxygen and unequally when
oxygen was short [@kerry2024rps24hypoxia]. Shifting the ratio toward the more
durable form helped cells survive and grow without enough oxygen, which makes
the splice choice consequential and not merely correlated
[@kerry2024rps24hypoxia].

In the brain the same gene reports on disease. One of the three forms is largely
confined to microglia and rises with age, with neurodegeneration, and after a
deliberate inflammatory challenge [@magadi2025rps24]. The increase was confirmed
at the protein level in human post-mortem brain from Alzheimer's disease,
Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease, and in mouse models of them
[@magadi2025rps24].

That confirmation depended on a reagent this book has not needed until now.
Antibodies were raised that tell the three protein ends apart, binding the
proline-lysine-glutamate form and not the ones ending in lysines
[@magadi2025rps24]. An antibody that distinguishes two proteins differing by
three residues is a proteoform-level reagent, and @sec-measuring explains why
such things are rare.

### RPS24 junctions as a cancer drug readout {#sec-rps24-cancer}

Across 135 lung cancer cell lines, two of the four junctions were present in
over 98 per cent of them, a third appeared in 89 lines, or 66 per cent, and the
muscle-associated one turned up in a single line [@nam2025rps24kras]. Most of
the arithmetically possible combinations are never built. Eight could be made
from three optional exons; three were found [@nam2025rps24kras].

Blocking KRAS in mutant lung cancer lines shifted the balance toward the form
carrying the three-base-pair exon, which those authors propose as a readout of
whether the drug is acting [@nam2025rps24kras]. That is in cell lines, and
nothing here shows it works in patients.

Resolving a three-base-pair difference took a deliberate method rather than a
standard pipeline. Separating the fragments by size distinguished isoforms
differing by a single base [@nam2025rps24kras]. The gene has a separate claim on
clinical attention too, since mutations in it are linked to Diamond-Blackfan
anaemia [@magadi2025rps24].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Both RPS24 sources need re-checking

The hypoxia work was read here as its bioRxiv preprint, although a version
exists in FEBS Letters, and the neurodegeneration work is preprint-only in this
corpus. Every number taken from either should be checked against the published
version. The microglial staining result is reported without a denominator here on
purpose: the text and the figure legend give different counts for the
Alzheimer's sections, and neither can be preferred from what was read.
:::

## Where this chapter leaves the protein question

Three things are now on firmer ground. The mechanism that produces an isoform
difference predicts which part of the protein changes. A difference confined to
untranslated sequence can change how much protein is made, and can change which
protein is made by moving the start codon the ribosome uses, though neither
follows reliably enough to be assumed. When the measurement is good enough to
see a gene's main product, it sees the gene's alternative products about as
often.

One thing remains unresolved, and it is
the thing a drug developer most needs. Knowing that an
isoform is translated somewhere, in some cell line, at some abundance, does not
establish that it is present in the tissue being treated, in enough copies, with
the epitope intact. That is the subject of @sec-measuring, and it is the gap
between this chapter and a therapy.
